improper-integrals-s1.title: The graph of $f(x) = \frac{6}{(x + 2)^2}$ for $x \ge 0$
improper-integrals-s1.text: Let $f(x) = \frac{6}{(x + 2)^2}$. The region $R$ lies under the graph of $f$, above the $x$-axis, and to the right of the $y$-axis; it goes on to the right without end.

plot.label: Graph of f(x) = 6/(x + 2) squared for x from 0 to 10, decreasing from 1.5 at x = 0 toward 0, with the region under it shaded all the way to the right edge

improper-integrals-s2.title: Areas from 1 to $b$ under two powers of $x$
improper-integrals-s2.text: The table gives $\int_1^b x^{-1/2}\,dx = 2\sqrt{b} - 2$ and $\int_1^b x^{-3/2}\,dx = 2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{b}}$ for several values of $b$.

table.caption: Values of two integrals from 1 to b

items.q: Which expression gives the area of $R$, written correctly?
options: $\lim_{b \to \infty} \frac{6}{(b + 2)^2}$
$\lim_{b \to \infty} \int_0^b \frac{6}{(x + 2)^2}\,dx$
That is the limit of the height of the graph, which is 0. The area is a limit of integrals, not of $f$.
$\infty$ is not a number to substitute. Arithmetic with $\infty$ earns no credit; write the limit.
The region is unbounded on the right, not at 0, and it does not stop at 10. The upper bound must go to $\infty$.
Right: an infinite limit of integration means a limit of definite integrals on $[0, b]$ as $b$ grows.

mistakes.why: $\int 6(x + 2)^{-2}\,dx = -6(x + 2)^{-1}$. Evaluate it as upper minus lower: $\lim_{b \to \infty}\left(-\frac{6}{b + 2} + \frac{6}{2}\right) = 3$.
$1.5 = f(0)$ is the height at the start, not the area. Integrate: $\lim_{b \to \infty}\left(3 - \frac{6}{b + 2}\right) = 3$.
Order of evaluation: upper minus lower, $-\frac{6}{b + 2} - \left(-\frac{6}{3}\right)$, which approaches $+2$.

items.q: A student says: "$f(x)$ approaches 0 as $x$ grows, so the area of $R$ has to be finite." Which response is correct?
options: Not enough: $\frac{1}{x}$ also approaches 0, yet $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x}$ diverges
The reason is enough: a graph that approaches 0 encloses a finite area
The conclusion is wrong: a region that goes on without end has infinite area
The reason is enough, and it holds because $f$ is also decreasing everywhere

why.correct: Convergence is decided by the limit of $\int_0^b f(x)\,dx$, not by the limit of $f(x)$. Here that limit is 3, so the integral converges, but for $\frac{1}{x}$ the same reasoning would fail.
options: Right: heights going to 0 do not settle it. The area of $R$ is finite because the limit of the integrals, 3, exists.
$y = \frac{1}{x}$ approaches 0, but its area from 1 to $b$ is $\ln b$, which grows without bound.
This region goes on without end and still has area 3. An unbounded region can have finite area.
$\frac{1}{x}$ is decreasing too, and its improper integral diverges. Decreasing toward 0 does not settle it.

items.q: Changing the exponent changes the answer. Which integral diverges?
options: $\int_0^\infty 6e^{-x}\,dx$
$\int_0^\infty \frac{6}{x + 2}\,dx$
$\int_0^\infty \frac{6}{(x + 2)^2}\,dx$
$\int_0^\infty \frac{6}{(x + 2)^3}\,dx$

why.correct: The power 1 gives a log, and $\ln(b + 2) \to \infty$. Powers above 1 and decaying exponentials give limits that exist.
options: $\int_0^b 6e^{-x}\,dx = 6 - 6e^{-b}$, which approaches 6: it converges.
Right: $\int_0^b \frac{6}{x + 2}\,dx = 6\ln(b + 2) - 6\ln 2$, which grows without bound.
This is the area of $R$, which converges to 3.
$\int_0^b 6(x + 2)^{-3}\,dx = \frac{3}{4} - \frac{3}{(b + 2)^2}$, which approaches $\frac{3}{4}$: it converges.

items.q: What do the formulas behind the table show as $b \to \infty$?
options: Both converge, because both integrands approach 0
Both diverge, because both columns keep increasing
$\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx$ converges to 2; $\int_1^\infty x^{-1/2}\,dx$ diverges
$\int_1^\infty x^{-1/2}\,dx$ converges to 2; $\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx$ diverges

why.correct: Read the limits of the formulas, not just the last row: $\lim_{b \to \infty}\left(2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{b}}\right) = 2$ and $\lim_{b \to \infty}\left(2\sqrt{b} - 2\right) = \infty$.
options: Integrands that approach 0 do not settle it: $2\sqrt{b} - 2$ grows without bound.
Increasing is not the same as unbounded: $2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{b}}$ increases but stays below 2.
Right: $2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{b}} \to 2$, while $2\sqrt{b} - 2 \to \infty$.
The columns are swapped: $x^{-1/2}$ gives $2\sqrt{b} - 2$, which keeps growing.

mistakes.why: $1.98$ is the value at $b = 10{,}000$. The improper integral is the limit as $b \to \infty$, exactly 2.

items.q: The table shows $p = \frac{1}{2}$ and $p = \frac{3}{2}$. For which $p$ does $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converge?
options: $p \ge 1$

why.correct: $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges to $\frac{1}{p - 1}$ when $p > 1$ and diverges when $p \le 1$.
options: At $p = 1$ the integral is $\ln b$, which grows without bound. The inequality is strict.
For $p < 1$ the antiderivative $\frac{x^{1 - p}}{1 - p}$ grows without bound, as the $p = \frac{1}{2}$ column shows.
$p = \frac{1}{2}$ is above 0 and its column diverges.
Right: for $p > 1$, $\int_1^b x^{-p}\,dx = \frac{1 - b^{1 - p}}{p - 1} \to \frac{1}{p - 1}$.

items.q: On $(0, 1]$, $x^{-1/2}$ is unbounded near 0. Find the value of $\int_0^1 x^{-1/2}\,dx$.

why.correct: The integrand is unbounded at 0, so take a limit there: $\lim_{a \to 0^+} \int_a^1 x^{-1/2}\,dx = \lim_{a \to 0^+}\left(2 - 2\sqrt{a}\right) = 2$. It converges, though the same power diverges on $[1, \infty)$.

mistakes.why: $\int xe^{-x}\,dx = -xe^{-x} - e^{-x}$; at $b$ it approaches 0, at 0 it is $-1$, and upper minus lower gives $0 - (-1) = 1$.
The value at the lower bound, $-0 \cdot e^0 - e^0 = -1$, is not 0. Subtracting it gives 1.

why.correct: Parts with $u = x$, $dv = e^{-x}\,dx$: $\lim_{b \to \infty}\left(-xe^{-x} - e^{-x}\right)\Big|_0^b = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left(-\frac{b}{e^b} - \frac{1}{e^b}\right) + 1 = 1$, since $\lim_{b \to \infty} \frac{b}{e^b} = \lim_{b \to \infty} \frac{1}{e^b} = 0$ by L'Hospital's rule.

items.q: A student writes $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = -\frac{1}{x}\Big|_{-1}^{1} = -2$. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The integral diverges: $\frac{1}{x^2}$ is unbounded at $x = 0$, and $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ diverges
The value $-2$ is right, by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
The value is $2$: the sign was lost
The value is 0, by symmetry about the $y$-axis

why.correct: An integrand unbounded inside the interval makes the integral improper: $\int_{-1}^{1} = \int_{-1}^{0} + \int_0^{1}$, and $\lim_{a \to 0^+} \int_a^1 x^{-2}\,dx = \lim_{a \to 0^+}\left(\frac{1}{a} - 1\right) = \infty$.
options: Right: the piece on $[0, 1]$ is $\lim_{a \to 0^+}\left(-1 + \frac{1}{a}\right) = \infty$, so the whole integral diverges.
The Fundamental Theorem needs $\frac{1}{x^2}$ continuous on $[-1, 1]$, and it is not continuous at 0. A positive integrand cannot give $-2$.
No finite value is right. The integrand blows up at 0, inside the interval.
$\frac{1}{x^2}$ is even and positive; symmetry doubles the area, and each half diverges.

mistakes.why: Integrating $e^{-2x}$ divides by $-2$; it does not multiply by 2.

options: converges to $\ln\frac{1}{2}$
converges to $\ln 2$
diverges, because $\ln b \to \infty$
converges to 1
The sign is reversed: subtract the value at 1, $\ln\frac{1}{2}$, which adds $\ln 2$.
Right: $\left(\ln x - \ln(x + 1)\right)\Big|_1^b = \ln\frac{b}{b + 1} + \ln 2$, and $\ln\frac{b}{b + 1} \to \ln 1 = 0$.
$\ln b$ and $\ln(b + 1)$ both grow, but their difference $\ln\frac{b}{b + 1}$ approaches 0. Combine the logs before taking the limit.
$\frac{1}{x(x + 1)} = \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{x + 1}$ integrates to logs, not powers. The limit is $\ln 2$.
It converges to $\frac{1}{\ln 2}$
It converges to 0, because $\frac{1}{x\ln x} \to 0$
It diverges, because $\ln(\ln b) \to \infty$
It converges to $\ln(\ln 2)$
An antiderivative of $\frac{1}{x\ln x}$ is $\ln(\ln x)$, not $-\frac{1}{\ln x}$ (that one belongs to $\frac{1}{x(\ln x)^2}$).
An integrand approaching 0 does not make an integral converge, and a positive integrand cannot give 0.
Right: with $u = \ln x$, $\int_2^b \frac{dx}{x\ln x} = \ln(\ln b) - \ln(\ln 2)$, which grows without bound, if slowly.
$\ln(\ln 2)$ is the value of the antiderivative at the lower bound. The value at $b$, $\ln(\ln b)$, grows without bound.

mistakes.why: $\int (3 - x)^{-1/2}\,dx = -2\sqrt{3 - x}$ (the inside has derivative $-1$). Upper minus lower: $0 - (-2\sqrt{3}) = 2\sqrt{3}$.

why.correct: The integrand is unbounded at $x = 3$: $\lim_{b \to 3^-}\left(-2\sqrt{3 - x}\right)\Big|_0^b = \lim_{b \to 3^-}\left(-2\sqrt{3 - b} + 2\sqrt{3}\right) = 2\sqrt{3}$.

items.q: Which line evaluates $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ with notation that earns full credit?
options: $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = -\frac{1}{x}\Big|_1^\infty = -\frac{1}{\infty} + 1 = 1$
$\lim_{b \to \infty} \int_1^b \frac{dx}{x^2} = \left(-\frac{1}{x}\right)\Big|_1^b = 1 - \frac{1}{b} = 1$
$\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = 1 - 0 = 1$ since the curve approaches 0
$\lim_{b \to \infty} \int_1^b \frac{dx}{x^2} = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left(1 - \frac{1}{b}\right) = 1$

why.correct: Write the limit, carry it through each step, and take it at the end. Dropping it mid-line or writing $\frac{1}{\infty}$ loses the point even when the number is right.
options: $\infty$ is substituted as if it were a number. That is arithmetic with infinity, which the scoring guidelines do not accept.
The limit was dropped in the middle: $1 - \frac{1}{b}$ does not equal 1. Keep $\lim_{b \to \infty}$ until you take it.
No limit of integrals is shown, and the reason given (the curve approaches 0) does not decide convergence.
Right: the limit is written in every expression until it is taken.
